claims.text: High-temperature annealing in a reducing atmosphere introduces oxygen vacancies into crystalline, near-equiatomic multimetal solid-solution nanoparticles.
Introducing a controlled amount of oxygen vacancies enhances nanoparticle stability during operation at 773–1173 K.
Oxygen vacancies reduce lattice strain in the multielement solid solution.
Oxygen vacancies enhance cohesion between the constituent metal elements.
Reduced lattice strain and enhanced intermetal cohesion improve thermal stability.
Reduced lattice strain and enhanced intermetal cohesion decrease degradation during high-temperature operation.
Treated nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Treated nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
The intervention is compatible with catalytic nanoparticles having low noble-metal content.
The intervention is expected to apply to compositions capable of forming a stable multielement solid solution.
The optimal oxygen-vacancy amount and distribution remain to be determined experimentally.
The appropriate reducing atmosphere and annealing conditions remain to be determined experimentally.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as a metallic solid solution composed of metals, but the proposed mediator is an oxygen vacancy. No oxygen-containing lattice, oxide phase, or pre-existing oxygen sublattice in which such vacancies could form is specified, making the intervention-to-mediator description internally incompatible as written.
